- Tensiomyography (TMG) is part of the toolkit, with a documented setup/operations SOP, but that SOP is headed with the names of a prior Director and Associate Director of Applied Performance (Althoff, Nelson), not Eric, and current active use is unclear from this corpus. **Inferred (legacy document, status unclear)** [technologytemplatesop.md]

## Education and staff development

- HHPR 5355 ("Power, Speed, Agility, & Periodization in Training") is Eric's own graduate-level course, co-taught with Chris Ruf and Michael Wenger; grading is split across two exams (10% and 20%), a group training-plan project (20%), and lecture/lab participation (40%), with a practical (teach-back) component on exams. **Inferred (transcript, syllabus content)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.1]
- A standalone, 16-week Intern Sport Science Curriculum is proposed, deliberately separate from the Playbook so it can be distributed and revised on its own cycle, aligned to the NSCA Essentials of Sport Science (CPSS) textbook, and adapted from a Clemson model to Baylor's own technology stack (ForceDecks, Catapult, ForceFrame, NordBord, DynaMo, Perch, SmartSpeed, Polar) and to include football alongside Olympic-sport examples. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 5]
- Curriculum design principle: interns need both the "why" (conceptual education) and the "how" (hands-on technical training) each week, and should leave the program with a professional portfolio of real work products (dashboards, reports, presentations, infographics), not just device-operation checklists. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.1, 5.4]
- The proposed curriculum deliberately adds sessions on interdisciplinary collaboration with Athletic Medicine, Performance Nutrition, and Mental Health Services, reflecting Baylor's specific department structure (Applied Performance inside Health & Wellness) rather than copying Clemson's Olympic-sports-only framing. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 5.3]

---

## No material found

None. Every one of the sixteen required sections had at least some material. Several sections are thin, though, and should be read as gaps rather than settled positions: **Rehab and return to play**, **Injury risk and prevention**, **Recovery and sleep**, **Nutrition and body composition**, and **Coaching, skill acquisition and constraints-led approach**. See `interview-prep.md`.

---

## Tensions and contradictions

1. **The task's own premise doesn't fully hold.** Both class transcripts (Class 1 and Class 3) are diarized entirely under a single Fireflies speaker label, "Chris Ruf," for every line — including Class 3, which the Spring 2026 teaching schedule assigns solo to Rash (`spring-2026-teaching.md`: "Feb. 5 | Conditioning - Alactic-Aerobic | Rash"). Fireflies likely defaulted to the meeting organizer's name instead of doing real per-speaker diarization. This means roughly 30,000 words of the richest, most first-person material in this corpus cannot be confidently attributed to Rash specifically versus Ruf or Wenger. Every transcript-sourced bullet above is marked Inferred for this reason, even where the underlying statement is a confident, first-person claim.

2. **Department reporting model is not internally consistent.** The Playbook (p.6) frames Applied Performance as a peer discipline inside Health & Wellness that "enables" Athletics Performance, Athletic Medicine, Nutrition, and Mental Health to answer their own questions. But Week 1 course material lists "Applied Performance" as one of many training sub-categories nested under Athletic Performance itself (p.11), and the same transcript narration describes Rash's role as "helping program and plan the training" — a support-staff framing, not a peer-department framing. Which model actually governs day-to-day authority is not reconciled anywhere in these documents.

3. **Coach's-eye-first versus objective-first is argued both ways.** The course material repeatedly argues that "you don't need a fancy test... you have to have a good coach's eye" and criticizes the GPS/load-monitoring era for breeding a fear-driven under-training culture. Eric's own SportSmith writing moves the opposite direction on daily monitoring specifically: he replaced subjective wellness surveys with objective force-plate mRSI because subjective self-report couldn't be trusted. Both share a skepticism of trendy or convenient data, but they land on opposite defaults (trust the trained eye vs. require an objective number) for the daily-monitoring question specifically.

4. **The Assessment Manual (V12) reads as an older document than the current technology stack.** It builds its 1RM-estimation protocol around GymAware, and its CMJ description references a "contact mat" for jump height. The current Playbook technology stack and the Development Plan both center velocity-based training on Perch, not GymAware, and the current Force Plate Testing V3 protocol runs all CMJ variants exclusively on ForceDecks force plates, with no contact mat mentioned. This suggests the Assessment Manual predates the current VALD/Perch-centered stack and may be a legacy document rather than the currently operative protocol — worth confirming directly with Eric before treating any of its specifics as current practice.

5. **Testing cueing instructions conflict across two protocol documents for the same test.** The Assessment Manual's CMJ instructions say explicitly: "Do not coach the strategy of jumping." The current Force Plate Testing V3 protocol gives testers specific verbal cues to give athletes during CMJ, squat-jump, and hop-test administration ("keep chest up," "land softly," "land stiff-legged on only the toes"). These may be reconcilable (safety/technique cues vs. jump-strategy cues are different things), but the two documents read differently on how much a tester should say out loud.

6. **Two different anaerobic-threshold heart-rate methods appear back to back in the same slide deck without being reconciled.** One slide gives an age-based formula (max HR = 220-age for men, 226-age for women, threshold at ~85% of that), and the very next slides give a body-size-based table (big/medium/small athlete, ~165/170/175 bpm threshold) as the operational standard used elsewhere throughout the conditioning material. Which one is actually used day to day is not stated. [class-4-2026.md pp.27-29]

7. **The Development Plan's own critique cuts against the corpus it's part of.** It states the current Baylor Playbook "has no educational component whatsoever" and reads "like a vendor product reference manual," even though Eric personally co-teaches a full graduate-level course covering much of the same material the Playbook is missing. The department's teaching capacity clearly exists; it just hasn't been captured back into the Playbook or a formal intern curriculum yet.

8. **The Playbook's NordBord documentation has not caught up with practice.** The Playbook's Technology Overview and Workflows still document a full, unqualified, roster-style NordBord data-collection SOP. The SportSmith piece describes explicitly retiring roster-wide NordBord testing for football starting after January 2023, keeping it only for small, targeted return-to-play groups. The written SOP has not been updated to reflect that decision.

9. **A personally-stated periodization preference is stated inside an unreliable-speaker transcript.** "For me personally, this is a more preferential model to use" (about undulating over linear periodization) is a strong, direct, first-person preference claim — but it comes from the same unreliably-diarized Class 1 transcript described in Tension 1, so it cannot be confirmed as Eric's own stated preference without his direct confirmation.

10. **Older vs. current unit-goal templates show almost no adopted content.** The Geyer and Skodinski Unit Goal Programming Standards documents are staff-authored templates for individual sport programming philosophy; Geyer's is mostly filled in (periodization model, weekly split, KPI tests for softball), Skodinski's is nearly blank (just the section headers). Neither is attributed to Eric, and there's no equivalent document in this corpus showing Eric's own answers to the same template questions — a real gap if Flint wants Eric's own unit-goal-style programming philosophy in his own words.

30	Monday with an active-recovery session (medium/low load, aerobic and general conditioning),

14	# Residual Training Effects Last Different Numbers of Days for Different Motor Abilities
15	
16	**What it is** — The residual training effect is defined as "the retention of changes
17	induced by systematic workloads beyond a certain time period after the cessation of
18	training," a term Issurin attributes to Brian and James Counsilman (1991) (PDF p. 33,
19	printed p. 22). Issurin & Lustig (2004) is cited as the source of Table 1.6 (PDF p. 35,
20	printed p. 24), giving residual duration ± SD in days after cessation of training for each
21	motor ability: **aerobic endurance 30 ± 5 days**, **maximum strength 30 ± 5 days**,
22	**anaerobic glycolytic endurance 18 ± 4 days**, **strength endurance 15 ± 5 days**,
23	**maximum speed (alactic) 5 ± 3 days**. Table 1.6's own physiological-background column
24	lists aerobic endurance's residual as resting on increased aerobic enzymes, mitochondria,
25	muscle capillaries, hemoglobin capacity, glycogen storage, and fat-metabolism rate, and
26	maximum strength's on improved neural mechanism and muscle hypertrophy from fiber
27	enlargement, with no percentages attached in the table itself. Later in the text (PDF p. 35,
28	printed p. 24), Issurin gives a specific figure for one of those table items: aerobic
29	enzymes increase by 40-90% with training (Volkov, 1986; Fox et al., 1993; Wilmore & Costill,
30	1993). He contrasts this with much smaller local adaptations from sprint training:
31	phosphocreatine storage (+2-5%), peak lactate accumulation (+10-20%), and anaerobic enzymes
32	(+2-20%), given without a citation on that page. On the following page (PDF p. 36, printed
33	p. 25), Thorstensson (1988) is cited specifically for "relatively small increases" in
34	quickly available energy sources, ATP and phosphocreatine, and enzymes such as creatine
35	kinase, from highly concentrated sprint training.
36	
37	**Why it works** — Issurin states the mechanism directly (PDF pp. 35-36, printed pp. 24-25):
38	aerobic ability, supported by pronounced morphological and biochemical changes, is retained
39	"for a number of weeks at near-peak level," while anaerobic abilities, particularly maximum
40	sprint speed, "retain near-peak levels for much shorter periods" because peak speed's gains
41	are smaller and rest on "very delicate and highly precise neuro-muscular interactions, which
42	are relatively unstable and cannot be maintained at the highest level without specially
43	organized training." Maximum strength's comparably long residual is attributed to pronounced
44	morphological, biochemical, and neural changes: enlargement of muscle-fiber cross-sectional
45	area, hyperplasia, recruitment of previously inactive motor units, synchronization of their
46	activity, and increased motor-neuron discharge frequency (Zatsiorsky, 1995). Strength
47	endurance's residual is stated to depend on event duration and the degree of
48	anaerobic-resource mobilization; longer-duration strength endurance has a relatively longer
49	residual thanks to aerobic adaptation.
50	
51	**When to apply** — Sequencing which ability to develop first in a training stage (see
52	[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]). **Inference:** an ability
53	with a long residual (aerobic endurance, max strength, 30 ± 5 d) can be built early and
54	carried further without direct work than a short-residual one, but a stage longer than about
55	30 days after accumulation ends needs a retention dose (see Example); max speed (5 ± 3 d)
56	needs re-exposure close to competition. **Eric's baseline directly echoes half of this table:** "Training
57	residual effects set the retraining cadence: aerobic capacity and max strength both need
58	re-exposure roughly every 30 days; speed needs re-exposure roughly every 5 days or tissue
59	readiness for max-velocity work degrades" (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and
60	programming," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` p.27). This 30/30/5-day
61	pattern matches Issurin's 30±5 / 30±5 / 5±3 figures because it is this table:
62	week1-lecture.md (marker p.66) reproduces Table 1.6 directly, under a slide block that names
63	"Issurin (Block Training Text)" as a source (marker p.64), and gives strength endurance as
64	~12 days against Issurin's 15±5, the one value where the course departs from the book.
65	
66	**When NOT to apply** — Treat the numbers as a synthesized rule of thumb
67	(±5, ±4, ±5, ±3 day spreads are themselves wide relative to the means), not a precise
68	per-athlete clock; Issurin does not report the sample or method behind Issurin & Lustig
69	(2004) in this text, so the table's evidentiary base cannot be checked further from this
70	source alone. Issurin's own surrounding text also notes limits on how far residual-effect
71	thinking travels: maximum oxygen uptake in highly trained endurance athletes falls when
72	weekly training volume drops below a certain level (Steinacker, 1993; Steinacker et al.,
73	1998), and large volumes of highly intense exercise do not prevent detraining and loss of
74	aerobic endurance during a taper (Mujika, 1999) (PDF p. 34, printed p. 23).
75	
76	**Contested, flag this directly to Eric:** a *different* part of the same baseline corpus
77	states the opposite ordering for detraining rate: "the traits easiest to build (aerobic) are
78	lost fastest under detraining; the traits hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest"
79	(`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems," citing `class-4-2026.md` p.47).
80	This conflicts with Table 1.6 (aerobic residual is the *longest*, tied with strength, at
81	30±5 days, while alactic speed is the *shortest* at 5±3 days). The class-1 transcript is
82	not a third, independent data point against class-4-2026.md: it also states that aerobic
83	capacity is gained and lost very quickly (marker pp.25, 28), gives its 30-day retention
84	windows as conditional on "a small retention load" continuing during that window (marker
85	p.28), a different construct from Issurin's residual *after cessation* of training, and
86	ties its 5-day speed figure to connective-tissue and nervous-system readiness ("otherwise
87	the nervous system doesn't change a whole lot," marker p.28) rather than to speed itself
88	decaying in 5 days. The course's own numbers come directly from this table (week1-lecture.md
89	marker pp.64, 66, strength endurance given there as ~12 days against Issurin's 15±5). Resolve
90	with Eric: this may be residual effect after cessation (Issurin, Table 1.6) versus rate of
91	loss without any retention dose (class-4-2026.md), two different constructs the corpus does
92	not itself reconcile. Do not harmonize these; record all three with their locators and keep
93	`contested`, with this as the stated reason.
94	
95	**Inference:** this table also converges with, but is not identical to, the vault's
96	Verkhoshansky-staging entry on heterochronic adaptation
97	([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]],
98	staging), which describes a *different* mechanism (order of biochemical sub-processes
99	gained/lost) rather than absolute day-counts per motor ability; both describe
100	heterochronicity in de-training, but at different levels of description; do not treat them
101	as restating the same specific claim.
102	
103	**Example** — **Inference:** in a training stage that opens with 4 weeks of accumulation
104	(building aerobic base and max strength) followed by 3 weeks of transmutation and 2 weeks of
105	realization, competition falls 35 days after accumulation ends: at the outer edge of the
106	aerobic and strength residuals' 30 ± 5-day window, not safely inside it. A coach relying on
107	this table would want a maintenance dose of both qualities somewhere in transmutation, not
108	an assumption that accumulation-phase gains are still fully in hand. Maximum speed work
109	needs re-introduction within about 5 days of the target competition, or its residual will
110	have decayed well below peak by competition day.
111	
112	**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
113	[[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]] (a ratio-based rule for
114	fatigue-vs-fitness decay, distinct from this table's absolute per-ability day counts:
115	cross-reference, do not conflate),
116	[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]] (staging),
117	[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]] (staging).
118

per-athlete clock; Issurin does not report the sample or method behind Issurin & Lustig

source alone. Issurin's own surrounding text also notes limits on how far residual-effect
thinking travels: maximum oxygen uptake in highly trained endurance athletes falls when
weekly training volume drops below a certain level (Steinacker, 1993; Steinacker et al.,
1998), and large volumes of highly intense exercise do not prevent detraining and loss of
aerobic endurance during a taper (Mujika, 1999) (PDF p. 34, printed p. 23).

**Contested, flag this directly to Eric:** a *different* part of the same baseline corpus
states the opposite ordering for detraining rate: "the traits easiest to build (aerobic) are
lost fastest under detraining; the traits hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest"
(`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems," citing `class-4-2026.md` p.47).

windows as conditional on "a small retention load" continuing during that window (marker
p.28), a different construct from Issurin's residual *after cessation* of training, and
ties its 5-day speed figure to connective-tissue and nervous-system readiness ("otherwise
the nervous system doesn't change a whole lot," marker p.28) rather than to speed itself
decaying in 5 days. The course's own numbers come directly from this table (week1-lecture.md
marker pp.64, 66, strength endurance given there as ~12 days against Issurin's 15±5). Resolve
with Eric: this may be residual effect after cessation (Issurin, Table 1.6) versus rate of
loss without any retention dose (class-4-2026.md), two different constructs the corpus does
not itself reconcile. Do not harmonize these; record all three with their locators and keep
`contested`, with this as the stated reason.

**Inference:** this table also converges with, but is not identical to, the vault's
Verkhoshansky-staging entry on heterochronic adaptation
([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]],
staging), which describes a *different* mechanism (order of biochemical sub-processes
gained/lost) rather than absolute day-counts per motor ability; both describe
heterochronicity in de-training, but at different levels of description; do not treat them
as restating the same specific claim.

realization, competition falls 35 days after accumulation ends: at the outer edge of the

an assumption that accumulation-phase gains are still fully in hand. Maximum speed work
needs re-introduction within about 5 days of the target competition, or its residual will
have decayed well below peak by competition day.

[[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]] (a ratio-based rule for
fatigue-vs-fitness decay, distinct from this table's absolute per-ability day counts:
cross-reference, do not conflate),

# The Pre-Competitive Microcycle: Cut Volume Hard, Raise Maximal-Speed and Sport-Specific Work, Keep Frequency

**What it is** — The pre-competitive microcycle forms the content of the realization
mesocycle (see [[framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription]]), and it is the
realization mesocycle itself, not this microcycle, that the book calls "traditionally...
termed the taper" (PDF p. 122, printed p. 111) (PDF pp. 104-105, printed pp. 93-94; verified
against page images, re-checked 2026-09-27). It must satisfy three demands (PDF p. 104, printed p. 93): sport-specific
exercises/tasks that simulate the forthcoming competition and build mental readiness and
toughness; development of maximal speed/power and sport-specific quickness; and full (or
partial) restoration after the preceding transmutation mesocycle's fatiguing workloads. Table
3.5 (PDF p. 105, printed p. 94, verified against page image) gives seven prescriptive
characteristics: **workload volume**, substantially reduced, to create conditions for full
recovery; **volume of intense exercises specifically**, substantially reduced versus the
prior mesocycle, so total drill volume falls but quality rises; **contribution of maximum
speed/power exercises**, substantially **increased** (well-rested athletes respond better to
maximal-speed drills, and maximal-speed training residuals are the shortest of any ability, per
[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]); **contribution of
sport-specific tasks**, substantially increased (simulative tasks improve adaptation to
expected competitive stressors); **workout frequency**, usually kept **similar** to the
previous mesocycle (subdividing the same total work into more, smaller portions raises
quality per session even as volume falls); **organization**, a rational mix of group,
individual and mixed workouts, weighted somewhat more toward individual work than usual, so
athletes can attend to personal technical detail and coach rapport; **restoration**,
deliberately favorable conditions and an increased volume of restorative exercises/workouts,
since athletes have more free time and motivation to use it. Separately from the Table 3.5
list, Issurin states that in qualified athletes, "particularly during the pre-competitive
training camp," maintaining frequency in practice means **eight to ten workouts per week**
even as volume per workout drops (PDF p. 106, printed p. 95; text, not a Table 3.5 cell).
Workout timing should match the expected competition's daily biological-rhythm window
(example given: Olympic canoe-kayak/rowing regattas run only in the morning, so pre-Olympic
training is scheduled to place peak-effort sessions at that same morning time, PDF p. 107,
printed p. 96). Figure 3.7 (PDF p. 108, printed p. 97; re-verified against the page image,
2026-09-27): sport-specific-simulation key-workouts fall on Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday
mornings (the expected competition time), alactic and technical work on the other mornings,
maximal or explosive strength on Monday and Thursday afternoons at medium load, and low-load
rest or alactic sessions on the other afternoons. The morning sport-specific simulations are
the point of the design, because the chart is built for morning peak performance (PDF p. 107,
printed p. 96); strength sits on two afternoons, not on a late-week ramp. On strength work
specifically, Issurin notes a real disagreement in the field: many athletes (particularly
swimmers, per Platonov & Fesenko, 1990, and also reported among volleyball and tennis players)
report high-resistance work pre-competition degrades fine technical skill, arguing for
reducing or excluding it; but sport-specific maximal/explosive strength work is also argued to
maintain the technical force component (Bompa & Carrera, 2003) and to prevent uncontrolled,
stress-hormone-driven muscle-mass loss pre-competition. The muscle-mass-protection point
specifically ("proper exercises for muscular hypertrophy prevent the uncontrolled reduction of
muscle mass induced by stress hormones") is given uncited in the text, separate from the
Bompa & Carrera citation for the technical-force-component point (PDF p. 108, printed p. 97).

**Why it works** — Reduced total load is stated as the "principal condition" for reaching
supercompensation before competition (PDF p. 106, printed p. 95); the two things this
recovered state is then spent on, maximal-speed drills and sport-specific simulation, are
each chosen because their quality specifically depends on a well-rested nervous system and
energy-resource availability (maximal speed) or on the athlete's capacity to fully attend to
technical/tactical detail under simulated competitive stress (sport-specific tasks). Issurin gives both sides on keeping frequency while cutting volume, not a single "quality
lever" argument: reduced frequency "can be considered as a way to decrease total workloads and
to find more time for restoration," but frequency is nonetheless usually kept because
"additional free time... can be a serious disadvantage" for athletes, alongside the more,
shorter, higher-quality-session logic (PDF p. 106, printed p. 95).

**When to apply — Inference, mapped to a college football calendar** — **Bowl prep:** the
week(s) immediately before a bowl game map most directly onto this framework: cut total
practice/lift volume hard, hold practice frequency roughly where it has been, shift the
practice mix toward maximal-speed/explosive work and heavy game-plan (sport-specific)
simulation, and weight walkthroughs/individual work more than a normal week. **In-season
tuning week:** the standard in-season game week already functions as a compressed version of
this pattern (practice volume tapers toward the game, Thursday/Friday sessions shift toward
walkthrough-intensity techno-tactical work); see
[[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]] for the specific team-sport
adaptation Issurin gives later in this chapter. **Season opener after fall camp:** the final
camp week before the opener is a pre-competitive microcycle relative to the whole camp block:
volume should come down from camp peak even though frequency (practice count) may stay similar.
The strength-during-taper disagreement Issurin reports (reduce high-resistance work vs. keep
sport-specific strength to protect force and prevent hormone-driven muscle loss) is directly
relevant to the recurring question of whether to lift heavy in bowl-prep week; this text does
not resolve it and presents both positions as live in the field. **Eric's baseline** gives no
session-frequency rule for a taper anywhere in `method-baseline.md`; the closest material is
the general in-season rule "maintain intensity, reduce volume" (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength
and power," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.20-21), which agrees directionally
(reduce volume, don't reduce intensity/speed work) but does not specify a frequency-holding
rule, an eight-to-ten-sessions-per-week figure, or an explicit sport-specific-task ramp; this
entry supplies that missing numeric structure, not something already adopted.

**When NOT to apply** — Every numeric particular in Table 3.5 (the
"substantially reduced/increased" volume and speed contributions) and the separately-stated
8-10 workouts/week figure are Issurin's own applied synthesis with no cited dose-response
study behind the specific numbers; he acknowledges directly that "many contradictions exist
regarding workout duration and frequency of high intensity exercises" in the
pre-competitive/taper literature generally (PDF p. 105, printed p. 94, citing Kubukeli et al.,
2002). **Inference, population caveat:** the worked example
(Figure 3.7) and both named case examples (Olympic canoe-kayak/rowing morning scheduling;
swimmer/volleyball/tennis strength-reduction reports) are individual, dual, or non-contact
sports; none address a 100+ player roster with heterogeneous individual readiness, a fixed
practice-week structure set partly by NCAA rules, or the additional load of team walkthroughs
and special-teams reps that a football pre-competitive week must still include. Issurin does
address team sports elsewhere in this same organization discussion: "in team sports...
group workouts are dominant" (PDF p. 106, printed p. 95), which this entry's individual/dual
framing does not capture. **Inference:** the "8-10 workouts per week" frequency figure, stated
for "qualified athletes, particularly during the pre-competitive training camp," assumes an
individual/dual-sport training camp structure and should not be read as a literal
session-count target for a football bowl-prep week. Issurin does not address game-week
travel, opponent scouting load, or academic-calendar constraints anywhere in this framework.

**Example** — **Inference:** a bowl-prep week could hold practice count similar to a normal in-season week
while cutting total practice/lift volume substantially, shifting a larger share of practice
time to explosive/speed work and full-speed game-plan simulation than a mid-season week would
carry, and deliberately expanding individual position-group time (film, technique correction)
relative to full-team periods, while treating the "how much to lift" question as an open
disagreement the source itself does not resolve, not a settled rule.

**Related** — [[framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription]],
[[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]],
[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]],
[[framework--microcycle-types-and-load-wave-design]],
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]] (staging),
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]] (staging,
`contested`: this entry's supercompensation mechanism, see Why it works, is the same model
that entry critiques).

14:# Evans's Own Caveat: the Fitness-Fatigue Model Is "Just a Concept," Not an Empirically Validated Model
16:**What it is** — Evans's slide (U1 L5 p.3-4) introduces the Fitness-Fatigue Model ("Fatigue
20:qualities together. JUST A CONCEPT" (capitalization as on the slide). He does not cite a
---BC

# Concentrated Loading and Planned Overreaching

**What it is** — A short period of deliberately high, "saturated" training load on one quality (planned overreaching), followed by restitution. Performance is *suppressed* during the loading block and rebounds — supercompensates — afterward. Siff and Verkhoshansky note gains may appear **4 to 12 weeks** after the concentrated block ends; the longer/larger the loading, the longer the delay before performance lifts. The **conjugated sequence** extends this: concentrate on one emphasis (e.g. strength) while holding maintenance loads elsewhere, then shift emphasis in the unloading block so a different quality rises.

**Why it works** — Saturating a stimulus drives a deeper adaptive signal than steady loading. Monitoring via the **testosterone:cortisol (T:C) ratio** tracks the anabolic–catabolic balance: ≥3 weeks of concentrated load lowers the basal T:C ratio (a catabolic shift, reduced preparedness); returning load to normal lets the T:C ratio and performance supercompensate. T:C indexes *preparedness*, not overtraining per se.

**When to apply** — Advanced athletes who can tolerate high loads; building a potent stimulus before a taper/peak; reducing long-term work volume versus concurrent training; timing a delayed performance rebound to a competition window.

**When NOT to apply** — Not for novices or athletes without the training capacity to absorb saturating loads — fatigue is substantial during accumulation and mismanagement tips into overtraining. The delayed-rebound timing (4–12 wk) must be planned backward from competition, or the peak lands in the wrong week. Builds on [[principle--supercompensation-cycle]] and [[framework--step-loading-paradigm]]; bounded by [[principle--individualization]].

**Example** — A 3-week strength-concentrated block (strength up, speed maintained) is timed so the performance rebound surfaces ~4–6 weeks later at the first key competition; T:C ratio is monitored to confirm the post-block recovery.
---SC

# The Supercompensation Cycle

**What it is** — After a training stimulus the body passes through four phases: (I) fatigue/homeostasis drop, 1–2 hr; (II) compensation/recovery, 24–48 hr; (III) supercompensation — a rebound *above* baseline, ~36–72 hr; (IV) involution — the gain fades if no new stimulus arrives, 3–7 days. Training the next stimulus into the supercompensation window raises the homeostatic set-point over time. Also called Weigert's law; Bompa links it to Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (alarm → resistance → exhaustion).

**Why it works** — A bout depletes substrates (glycogen, PCr), accumulates fatigue and cortisol, and transiently lowers force output. Given adequate recovery the body overshoots when restoring those reserves, establishing a new, higher baseline. Protein synthesis is elevated +50% by 4 hr and +109% by 24 hr post-resistance-bout.

**When to apply** — Sequencing hard sessions and recovery; justifying why intensities must alternate (high/moderate/low); timing the next stressor to land on the rebound, not the trough.

**When NOT to apply** — Don't treat it as a precise single-factor clock. Recovery windows vary enormously by session type (6–8 hr for medium aerobic work; >48 hr for high-CNS work) and by athlete training status, nutrition, and contraction type (eccentric/SSC fatigue recovers bimodally, full recovery 6–8 days). Contemporary sport science largely prefers the **fitness–fatigue (two-factor) model** over literal supercompensation; treat this as a useful mental model, not a measured prescription. See [[principle--progressive-overload-threshold]] and [[heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]].

**Example** — After a heavy lower-body session that depletes glycogen and induces DOMS, scheduling the next heavy lower session ~48–72 hr later (not at 24 hr) aims to load the supercompensation rebound rather than residual fatigue.

content.content:
## Key findings

- Most conventional CMJ variables and several alternative concentric/eccentric variables met both reliability criteria within and between sessions under both protocols. [p. 10]
- Conventional measures such as concentric mean force, mean power, peak force, flight time, and jump height generally showed strong reliability, while flight-time-to-contraction-time ratio was less reliable with arm swing between sessions. [p. 5]
- Several phase-duration and rate-of-force-development variables failed one or both reliability thresholds, with some coefficients of variation exceeding 20% and some ICCs below 0.70. [pp. 6-9]
- The authors interpreted the no-arm-swing protocol as better suited to isolating lower-extremity function and acute readiness/fatigue, while arm swing may better represent longer-term changes in sport-specific jump performance. [p. 10] [p. 12]

## Limitations and applicability

- Training load during the testing period was not directly quantified; matching court time was used as an indirect control. [p. 12]
- The cohort was small and relatively homogeneous, which can suppress between-athlete variability and reduce ICC estimates even when absolute repeatability is acceptable. [p. 12]
- The study evaluated reliability, not whether a variable is sensitive or specific to meaningful fatigue, adaptation, or performance change. [p. 12]
- Only single-measure ICCs were emphasized; averaging trials may improve reliability but changes the operational testing contract. [p. 11]
- Additional transfer limitation (practitioner interpretation): results from skilled Division I basketball players do not automatically generalize to other sports, development levels, or testing hardware and analysis settings.

## Practitioner interpretation

Choose and standardize the CMJ protocol around the monitoring question. A no-arm-swing jump can reduce upper-body contribution when the goal is lower-extremity readiness; an arm-swing jump may offer a more sport-like expression for longer-term performance profiling. Do not mix protocols in a longitudinal series, and do not select a metric solely because it is available or reliable—establish local typical error and confirm that the measure changes meaningfully for the intended decision.

## Evidence map

| Claim | Locator | Evidence type |
|---|---|---|
| Randomized two-session protocol | pp. 4-5 | method |
| Reliability thresholds | p. 9 | method |
| Reliability of conventional CMJ outcomes | p. 5; p. 10 | result |
| Poorer reliability of several alternative rate/duration measures | pp. 6-9 | result |
| Intended arm-swing versus no-arm-swing applications | p. 10; p. 12 | author application |
| Unmeasured load, homogeneous sample, and responsiveness gap | p. 12 | limitation |

1. J Strength Cond Res. 2011 Oct;25(10):2653-60. doi:
10.1519/JSC.0b013e31822dcd96.
Effects of in-season strength maintenance training frequency in professional 
soccer players.
Rønnestad BR(1), Nymark BS, Raastad T.
(1)Lillehammer University College, Lillehammer, Norway. bent.ronnestad@hil.no
The aim of the present study was to examine the effect of in-season strength 
maintenance training frequency on strength, jump height, and 40-m sprint 
performance in professional soccer players. The players performed the same 
strength training program twice a week during a 10-week preparatory period. 
In-season, one group of players performed 1 strength maintenance training 
session per week (group 2 + 1; n = 7), whereas the other group performed 1 
session every second week (group 2 + 0.5; n = 7). Only the strength training 
frequency during the in-season differed between the groups, whereas the 
exercise, sets and number of repetition maximum as well as soccer sessions were 
similar in the 2 groups. The preseason strength training resulted in an 
increased strength, sprint, and jump height (p < 0.05). During the first 12 
weeks of the in-season, the initial gain in strength and 40-m sprint performance 
was maintained in group 2 + 1, whereas both strength and sprint performance were 
reduced in group 2 + 0.5 (p < 0.05). There was no statistical significant change 
in jump height in any of the 2 groups during the first 12 weeks of the 
in-season. In conclusion, performing 1 weekly strength maintenance session 
during the first 12 weeks of the in-season allowed professional soccer players 
to maintain the improved strength, sprint, and jump performance achieved during 
a preceding 10-week preparatory period. On the other hand, performing only 1 
strength maintenance session every second week during the in-season resulted in 
reduced leg strength and 40-m sprint performance. The practical recommendation 
from the present study is that during a 12-week period, 1 strength maintenance 
session per week may be sufficient to maintain initial gain in strength and 
sprint performance achieved during a preceding preparatory period.
2. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2007 Aug;39(8):1358-65. doi:
10.1249/mss.0b013e31806010e0.
Effects of tapering on performance: a meta-analysis.
Bosquet L(1), Montpetit J, Arvisais D, Mujika I.
(1)Department of Kinesiology, University of Montreal, Montreal, Canada. 
laurent.bosquet@montreal.ca
PURPOSE: The purpose of this investigation was to assess the effects of 
alterations in taper components on performance in competitive athletes, through 
a meta-analysis.
METHODS: Six databases were searched using relevant terms and strategies. 
Criteria for study inclusion were that participants must be competitive 
athletes, a tapering intervention must be employed providing details about the 
procedures used to decrease the training load, use of actual competition or 
field-based criterion performance, and inclusion of all necessary data to 
calculate effect sizes. Datasets reported in more than one published study were 
only included once in the present analyses. Twenty-seven of 182 potential 
studies met these criteria and were included in the analysis. The dependent 
variable was performance, and the independent variables were the decrease in 
training intensity, volume, and frequency, as well as the pattern of the taper 
and its duration. Pre-post taper standardized mean differences in performance 
were calculated and weighted according to the within-group heterogeneity to 
develop an overall effect.

and Foulis, SA. J Strength Cond Res 35(5): 1449-1458, 2021-Nearly every 
physically active person encounters periods in which the time available for 
exercise is limited (e.g., personal, family, or business conflicts). During such 
periods, the goal of physical training may be to simply maintain (rather than 
improve) physical performance. Similarly, certain special populations may desire 
to maintain performance for prolonged periods, namely athletes (during the 
competitive season and off-season) and military personnel (during deployment). 
The primary purpose of this brief, narrative review is to identify the minimal 
dose of exercise (i.e., frequency, volume, and intensity) needed to maintain 
physical performance over time. In general populations, endurance performance 
can be maintained for up to 15 weeks when training frequency is reduced to as 
little as 2 sessions per week or when exercise volume is reduced by 33-66% (as 
low as 13-26 minutes per session), as long as exercise intensity (exercising 
heart rate) is maintained. Strength and muscle size (at least in younger 
populations) can be maintained for up to 32 weeks with as little as 1 session of 
strength training per week and 1 set per exercise, as long as exercise intensity 
(relative load) is maintained; whereas, in older populations, maintaining muscle 
size may require up to 2 sessions per week and 2-3 sets per exercise, while 
maintaining exercise intensity. Insufficient data exists to make specific 
recommendations for athletes or military personnel. Our primary conclusion is 
that exercise intensity seems to be the key variable for maintaining physical 
performance over time, despite relatively large reductions in exercise frequency 
and volume.

(1)Department of Research and Development, Medical Services, Athletic Club of 
Bilboa, Basque Country, Spain. imujika@grn.es
The taper is a progressive nonlinear reduction of the training load during a 
variable period of time, in an attempt to reduce the physiological and 
psychological stress of daily training and optimize sports performance. The aim 
of the taper should be to minimize accumulated fatigue without compromising 
adaptations. This is best achieved by maintaining training intensity, reducing 
the training volume (up to 60-90%) and slightly reducing training frequency (no 
more than 20%). The optimal duration of the taper ranges between 4 and more than 
28 d. Progressive nonlinear tapers are more beneficial to performance than step 
tapers. Performance usually improves by about 3% (usual range 0.5-6.0%), due to 
positive changes in the cardiorespiratory, metabolic, hematological, hormonal, 
neuromuscular, and psychological status of the athletes.

The aim of the present study was to examine the effect of in-season strength 
maintenance training frequency on strength, jump height, and 40-m sprint 
performance in professional soccer players. The players performed the same 
strength training program twice a week during a 10-week preparatory period. 
In-season, one group of players performed 1 strength maintenance training 
session per week (group 2 + 1; n = 7), whereas the other group performed 1 
session every second week (group 2 + 0.5; n = 7). Only the strength training 
frequency during the in-season differed between the groups, whereas the 
exercise, sets and number of repetition maximum as well as soccer sessions were 
similar in the 2 groups. The preseason strength training resulted in an 
increased strength, sprint, and jump height (p < 0.05). During the first 12 
weeks of the in-season, the initial gain in strength and 40-m sprint performance 
was maintained in group 2 + 1, whereas both strength and sprint performance were 
reduced in group 2 + 0.5 (p < 0.05). There was no statistical significant change 
in jump height in any of the 2 groups during the first 12 weeks of the 
in-season. In conclusion, performing 1 weekly strength maintenance session 
during the first 12 weeks of the in-season allowed professional soccer players 
to maintain the improved strength, sprint, and jump performance achieved during 
a preceding 10-week preparatory period. On the other hand, performing only 1 
strength maintenance session every second week during the in-season resulted in 
reduced leg strength and 40-m sprint performance. The practical recommendation 
from the present study is that during a 12-week period, 1 strength maintenance 
session per week may be sufficient to maintain initial gain in strength and 
sprint performance achieved during a preceding preparatory period.

1. Sports Med. 2000 Aug;30(2):79-87. doi: 10.2165/00007256-200030020-00002.
Detraining: loss of training-induced physiological and performance adaptations. 
Part I: short term insufficient training stimulus.
Mujika I(1), Padilla S.
Bilbao, Basque Country, Spain. imujika@grn.es
Detraining is the partial or complete loss of training-induced adaptations, in 
response to an insufficient training stimulus. Detraining characteristics may be 
different depending on the duration of training cessation or insufficient 
training. Short term detraining (less than 4 weeks of insufficient training 
stimulus) is analysed in part I of this review, whereas part II will deal with 
long term detraining (more than 4 weeks of insufficient training stimulus). 
Short term cardiorespiratory detraining is characterised in highly trained 
athletes by a rapid decline in maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max) and blood volume. 
Exercise heart rate increases insufficiently to counterbalance the decreased 
stroke volume, and maximal cardiac output is thus reduced. Ventilatory 
efficiency and endurance performance are also impaired. These changes are more 
moderate in recently trained individuals. From a metabolic viewpoint, short term 
inactivity implies an increased reliance on carbohydrate metabolism during 
exercise, as shown by a higher exercise respiratory exchange ratio, and lowered 
lipase activity, GLUT-4 content, glycogen level and lactate threshold. At the 
muscle level, capillary density and oxidative enzyme activities are reduced. 
Training-induced changes in fibre cross-sectional area are reversed, but 
strength performance declines are limited. Hormonal changes include a reduced 
insulin sensitivity, a possible increase in testosterone and growth hormone 
levels in strength athletes, and a reversal of short term training-induced 
adaptations in fluid-electrolyte regulating hormones.

Performance.

intensities but equal volume reductions on neuromuscular performance.
METHODS: Eleven strength-trained men (21.3 [3.3] y, 92.3 [17.6] kg, relative 
1-repetition-maximum deadlift 1.9 [0.2] times bodyweight) completed a crossover 
study. Specifically, two 4-wk strength-training blocks were followed by a taper 
week with reduced volume (∼70%) involving either increased (5.9%) or decreased 
posttaper (T3). Salivary testosterone and cortisol, plasma creatine kinase, a 
Daily Analysis of Life Demands in Athletes questionnaire, countermovement jump 
RESULTS: CMJ height improved significantly over time (P < .001), with 
significant increases from T1 (38.0 [5.5] cm) to both T2 (39.3 [5.3] cm; 
P = .010) and T3 (40.0 [5.3] cm; P = .001) and from T2 to T3 (P = .002). CMJ 
flight time:contraction time increased significantly over time (P = .004), with 
significant increases from T1 (0.747 [0.162]) to T2 (0.791 [0.163]; P = .012). 
Isometric midthigh-pull relative peak force improved significantly over time 
[4.8] N/kg; P = .013). No significant changes were found between tapers. 
However, the higher-intensity taper produced small effect-size increases at T3 
vs T1 for isometric midthigh-pull relative peak force, CMJ height, and flight 
time:contraction time, while the lower-intensity taper only produced small 
effect-size improvements at T3 vs T1 for CMJ height.
CONCLUSIONS: A strength-training taper with volume reductions had a positive 
effect on power, with a tendency for the higher-intensity taper to produce more 
favorable changes in strength and power.

Peaking for optimal performance: Research limitations and future directions.
Pyne DB(1), Mujika I, Reilly T.
David.pyne@ausport.gov.au
A key element of the physical preparation of athletes is the taper period in the 
weeks immediately preceding competition. Existing research has defined the 
taper, identified various forms used in contemporary sport, and examined the 
prescription of training volume, load, intensity, duration, and type 
combative, racquet, and precision (target) sports; the relatively small number 
of randomized controlled trials; the narrow focus on a single competition 
events; and limited understanding of the physiological, neuromuscular, and 
biomechanical basis of the taper. Future research should address these 
limitations, together with the influence of prior training on optimal tapering 
strategies, and the interactions between the taper and long-haul travel, heat, 
and altitude. Practitioners seek information on how to prescribe tapers from 
season to season during an athlete's career, or a team's progression through a 
domestic league season, or multi-year Olympic or World Cup cycle. Practical 
guidelines for planning effective tapers for the Vancouver 2010 and London 2012 
Olympics will evolve from both experimental investigations and modelling of 
successful tapers currently employed in a wide range of sports.

Comparison between linear and nonlinear in-season training programs in freshman 
football players.
Hoffman JR(1), Wendell M, Cooper J, Kang J.
08628, USA. hoffmanj@tcnj.edu
The purpose of this study was to compare linear (LT) with nonlinear (NL) 
in-season training programs in freshman football players during the course of 2 
separate seasons. During the first year (n = 14, mean +/- SD = 177.3 +/- 4.8 cm, 
88.0 +/- 9.7 kg), the LT program was employed 2 days per week. In the second 
year (n = 14, 175.0 +/- 7.1 cm, 94.2 +/- 20.5 kg), a 2 days per week LT was 
used. Subjects were tested for maximal strength in the squat (1 repetition 
maximum [1RM]) and bench press (1RM) exercises. A significant improvement in 1RM 
squat was seen in LT, but not in NL. No significant improvement in 1RM bench 
press was seen in either group. A significant difference between LT and NL was 
observed in Delta1RM squat (13.8 +/- 7.4 kg compared with 1.6 +/- 2.6 kg, 
respectively). Results of this study suggest that LT may be more effective in 
eliciting strength gains than NL in freshman football players during an 
in-season training program.

5-day mid-season break on performance - an observational study.

BACKGROUND: Detraining is a partial reduction or total stoppage of training 
workloads, resulting in physical and physiological modifications. Prior studies 
have shown significant reductions in strength and power typically after 
long-term interruptions (i.e., > 4 weeks), whereas evidence for short-term 
detraining (i.e., < 4 weeks) remains inconclusive. This observational study 
describes acute changes in the physical abilities of football players associated 
with a 5-day in-season break under real-world conditions. METHODS: In this 
uncontrolled observational study, repeated sprinting ability (primary outcome), 
body composition, vertical jump performance, and maximum thigh adduction and 
abduction strength were assessed in 17–21 semi-professional male football 
players (n = 17 for the primary outcome; other tests ranged from 17 to 21) 
before and after a 5-day in-season break (age: 21.5 ± 1.37 years; height: 
178.96 ± 6.59 cm). Descriptive statistics and paired t-tests were used for 
comparisons. Intra-individual differences were also calculated. RESULTS: After 
the 5-day break, repeated sprinting ability was significantly worse. Total time 
to complete the RAST was approximately 1.0 s higher (before: 29.89 ± 1.14 s; 
after: 30.77 ± 1.62 s, p = 0.009, d = 0.634). Peak power and maximal velocity 
showed mean reductions of 55 watts (before: 892.34 ± 125.46 W; after: 
837.54 ± 108.92 W, p = 0.049, d = -0.427) and 0.65 km.hˉ¹ (before: 
26.86 ± 1.03 km.hˉ¹; after: 26.21 ± 1.35 km.hˉ¹, p = 0.030, d = -0.489), 
respectively, indicating small-to-moderate effect sizes. Vertical jump 
performance showed slight, non-significant improvements. No significant changes 
were found for maximum thigh strength or body composition. CONCLUSION: A brief 
5-day in-season break under uncontrolled, real-world conditions was associated 
with small-to-moderate impairments in repeated sprinting ability, while body 
composition, maximal strength, and vertical jump performance were largely 
maintained. These findings underscore the need for practitioners to prioritise 
targeted interventions for repeated sprinting ability following short in-season 
breaks, alongside strategies to restore performance without compromising 
technical-tactical demands.

Pyne DB(1), Mujika I, Reilly T.
David.pyne@ausport.gov.au
A key element of the physical preparation of athletes is the taper period in the 
weeks immediately preceding competition. Existing research has defined the 
taper, identified various forms used in contemporary sport, and examined the 
prescription of training volume, load, intensity, duration, and type 
combative, racquet, and precision (target) sports; the relatively small number 
of randomized controlled trials; the narrow focus on a single competition 
events; and limited understanding of the physiological, neuromuscular, and 
biomechanical basis of the taper. Future research should address these 
limitations, together with the influence of prior training on optimal tapering 
strategies, and the interactions between the taper and long-haul travel, heat, 
and altitude. Practitioners seek information on how to prescribe tapers from 
season to season during an athlete's career, or a team's progression through a 
domestic league season, or multi-year Olympic or World Cup cycle. Practical 
guidelines for planning effective tapers for the Vancouver 2010 and London 2012 
Olympics will evolve from both experimental investigations and modelling of 
successful tapers currently employed in a wide range of sports.

football players.
Hoffman JR(1), Wendell M, Cooper J, Kang J.
08628, USA. hoffmanj@tcnj.edu
The purpose of this study was to compare linear (LT) with nonlinear (NL) 
in-season training programs in freshman football players during the course of 2 
separate seasons. During the first year (n = 14, mean +/- SD = 177.3 +/- 4.8 cm, 
88.0 +/- 9.7 kg), the LT program was employed 2 days per week. In the second 
year (n = 14, 175.0 +/- 7.1 cm, 94.2 +/- 20.5 kg), a 2 days per week LT was 
used. Subjects were tested for maximal strength in the squat (1 repetition 
maximum [1RM]) and bench press (1RM) exercises. A significant improvement in 1RM 
squat was seen in LT, but not in NL. No significant improvement in 1RM bench 
press was seen in either group. A significant difference between LT and NL was 
observed in Delta1RM squat (13.8 +/- 7.4 kg compared with 1.6 +/- 2.6 kg, 
respectively). Results of this study suggest that LT may be more effective in 
eliciting strength gains than NL in freshman football players during an 
in-season training program.

5-day mid-season break on performance - an observational study.
Saldanha JG(1)(2)(3), Santos F(4)(5)(6), Martinho DV(6)(7), Sarmento H(6)(7),

BACKGROUND: Detraining is a partial reduction or total stoppage of training 
workloads, resulting in physical and physiological modifications. Prior studies 
have shown significant reductions in strength and power typically after 
long-term interruptions (i.e., > 4 weeks), whereas evidence for short-term 
detraining (i.e., < 4 weeks) remains inconclusive. This observational study 
describes acute changes in the physical abilities of football players associated 
with a 5-day in-season break under real-world conditions. METHODS: In this 
uncontrolled observational study, repeated sprinting ability (primary outcome), 
body composition, vertical jump performance, and maximum thigh adduction and 
abduction strength were assessed in 17–21 semi-professional male football 
players (n = 17 for the primary outcome; other tests ranged from 17 to 21) 
before and after a 5-day in-season break (age: 21.5 ± 1.37 years; height: 
178.96 ± 6.59 cm). Descriptive statistics and paired t-tests were used for 
comparisons. Intra-individual differences were also calculated. RESULTS: After 
the 5-day break, repeated sprinting ability was significantly worse. Total time 
to complete the RAST was approximately 1.0 s higher (before: 29.89 ± 1.14 s; 
after: 30.77 ± 1.62 s, p = 0.009, d = 0.634). Peak power and maximal velocity 
showed mean reductions of 55 watts (before: 892.34 ± 125.46 W; after: 
837.54 ± 108.92 W, p = 0.049, d = -0.427) and 0.65 km.hˉ¹ (before: 
26.86 ± 1.03 km.hˉ¹; after: 26.21 ± 1.35 km.hˉ¹, p = 0.030, d = -0.489), 
respectively, indicating small-to-moderate effect sizes. Vertical jump 
performance showed slight, non-significant improvements. No significant changes 
were found for maximum thigh strength or body composition. CONCLUSION: A brief 
5-day in-season break under uncontrolled, real-world conditions was associated 
with small-to-moderate impairments in repeated sprinting ability, while body 
composition, maximal strength, and vertical jump performance were largely 
maintained. These findings underscore the need for practitioners to prioritise 
targeted interventions for repeated sprinting ability following short in-season 
breaks, alongside strategies to restore performance without compromising 
technical-tactical demands.

  "abstract": "Peaking for major competition is considered critical for maximizing team-sport performance. However, there is little scientific information available to guide coaches in prescribing efficient tapering strategies for team-sport players.\nPurpose:To monitor the changes in physical performance in elite team-sport players during a 3-wk taper after a preseason training camp.\nMethods:Ten male international rugby sevens players were tested before (Pre) and after (Post) a 4-wk preseason training camp focusing on high-intensity training and strength training with moderate loads and once each week during a subsequent 3-wk taper. During each testing session, midthigh-pull maximal strength, sprint-acceleration mechanical outputs, and performance, as well as repeated-sprint ability (RSA), were assessed.\nResults:At Post, no single peak performance was observed for maximal lower-limb force output and sprint performance, while RSA peaked for only 1 athlete. During the taper, 30-m-sprint time decreased almost certainly (–3.1% ± 0.9%, large), while maximal lower-limb strength and RSA, respectively, improved very likely (+7.7% ± 5.3%, small) and almost certainly (+9.0% ± 2.6%, moderate). Of the peak performances, 70%, 80%, and 80% occurred within the first 2 wk of taper for RSA, maximal force output, and sprint performance, respectively.\nConclusions:These results show the sensitivity of physical qualities to tapering in rugby sevens players and suggest that an ~1- to 2-wk tapering time frame appears optimal to maximize the overall physical-performance response.",

{"result":[{"page":6,"text":"problematic due to the lack of similar investigations in NCAA
Division I football. Previous investigations in Australian football
have reported increased training loads and training session
duration in the preseason period when compared with the
in-season competitive period (23,26). Although similarities
may exist between Australian football and NCAA Division I
college football, direct comparisons between the preseason pe-
riods in each of these sports is problematic, most notably due to
the duration of the preseason period in Australian football,
often lasting more than 20 weeks (23), whereas college football
preseason practice takes place over approximately 4 weeks. In
NCAA Division I college football, GPS-derived positional
movement characteristics have been quantiﬁed (7,28), and bio-
chemical markers of muscle damage associated with preseason
training camp have been examined (8,14). However, research
has not attempted to quantify the differences that may exist
between practice loads encountered by NCAA Division I foot-
ball players during the preseason training camp with those
experienced during the in-season period, and previously this
information was limited to coaching intuition and anecdotal
reports. It is clear that the preseason training camp is a critical
period for football players, yet recommendations have not been
established which elucidate effective strategies for periodizing
preseason training camp practices to maximize the position-
speciﬁc
tactical,
technical,
and
physical
demands
while minimizing the deleterious effects of fatigue. Periodization
refers to the logical and systematic process of sequencing and
integrating training interventions to achieve peak performance
at the appropriate times (13). An ideology that highlights the
inﬂuence of a properly periodized period of training is referred
to as the stimulus-fatigue-recovery-adaptation theory, which
suggests that the greater the overall magnitude of the physical
demands, the more fatigue accumulates, and the longer the
recovery and adaptation processes take (13). When comparing
in-season to preseason practice demands, it is reasonable to
suggest that the fatigue associated with preseason training
camp practices in this study may require increased time to
recover from, and adapt to, the imposed demands.
In this study, an in-season week of training consisted of 3
practices and 1 game, whereas preseason 1 comprised 8
practice sessions in the ﬁrst 7 days, and as such, the
cumulative training load resulting from preseason 1 increased
compared with a typical in-season week of training. This
however, does not explain the signiﬁcantly (p # 0.05) greater
PLMean and PLMax reported for individual practice sessions
of preseason 1, which was likely the result of not only the
composition, but the duration of the practice sessions. A
greater portion of practice time in preseason 1 was devoted
to position-speciﬁc skills and techniques than on situational
and tactical planning in an offensive or defensive group set-
ting, which commonly occurs throughout in-season practice
sessions when preparing for competition. Individual skill work
takes place in smaller groups, and allows for increased fre-
quency of movement, potentially resulting in higher PL.
The mean session duration in preseason 1 was 145 minutes;
however, the ﬁrst practice session of preseason 1 was 169 mi-
nutes in duration, which represented the longest practice ses-
sion of the entire season. The signiﬁcant increases in PLMax
and PLMean that occurred during preseason 1 may therefore
be also attributed to the practice session duration. Previous
research (26) in Australian football has demonstrated that
reductions in session duration accompany similar reductions
in PL. Speciﬁcally, a 30% reduction in duration resulted in
a ;30% reduction in PL, and as such, periodizing practice
duration may be an effective strategy to reduce PL and facil-
itate between-session recovery to reduce injury risk and opti-
mize subsequent practice session performance.
The PLMax and PLMean values reported in preseason 2
were not signiﬁcantly different from preseason 3, however,
a signiﬁcant (p # 0.05) decrease in both PL measures was
demonstrated compared with preseason 1. Week 2 of presea-
son consisted of 8 practice sessions with an average practice
session duration of 123 minutes. Practice sessions in preseason
2 were programmed to provide less time dedicated to individ-
ual position-speciﬁc skill work and a larger amount of time to
periods of situational drills involving the entire offensive and
defensive teams. During the in-season period, the Tuesday
practice sessions were planned as the highest practice loads
of the week, and PL resulting from in-season Tuesday practices
were signiﬁcantly (p # 0.05) greater than PLMean in preseason
2 for weeks 2–8 during the in-season period. The PL associated
with the Tuesday practice session for in-season week 1 was
signiﬁcantly (p # 0.05) lower than the PLMean in preseason
2, the likely result of a reduction in session duration in an
attempt to mitigate any deleterious effect of fatigue that accu-
mulated in the preseason training camp. A similar pattern was
demonstrated for Wednesday practice sessions, whereby in-
season week 1, 10, 11, and 12 demonstrated signiﬁcantly (p
# 0.05) lower PL than the PLMean reported in preseason 2.
These ﬁndings illustrate that coaches may intuitively reduce
practice loads during in-season, particularly in the latter part,
to maintain the physical capacities developed throughout the
preseason and early in-season periods, but to also provide ade-
quate recovery to support optimal gameday performance.
A comparison of PLMean from preseason 3 practice
sessions with PL resulting from in-season Tuesday and
Wednesday practice sessions reveals a decrease in training
loads for weeks 9–12 of the season. This seems to be the
result of a preplanned reduction in session duration for Tues-
day and Wednesday practices in the last 4 weeks of the
season. Similar reductions in PL associated with Thursday
practices sessions for the last 4 weeks of the season were not
demonstrated, most likely due to the consistent nature of
load programming for Thursday practice sessions.
An examination of the cumulative weekly PL revealed
signiﬁcantly (p # 0.05) greater cumulative PL for preseason 1
than preseason 2 and 3, and signiﬁcantly (p # 0.05) greater
cumulative PL for preseason 2 than preseason 3. In addition, all
preseason weeks were associated with signiﬁcantly (p # 0.05)
greater
cumulative
PL
than
all
in-season
weeks.

# Review: peaking and taper synthesis note

Method. Every [[link]] was opened in `SecondBrain/Knowledge/library` and its `confidence:` checked. All 12 book-entry confidence tags in the note match the entries. External claims were checked against PubMed abstracts (efetch: Ronnestad 2011, Bosquet 2007, Vachon 2021, Spiering 2021, Mujika and Padilla 2003, Mujika and Padilla 2000 Part I, Pritchard 2019, Pyne 2009, Hoffman 2003, Saldanha 2026), the Bond portal abstract (Pritchard 2015), and Zotero page reads (Wellman 396EV93N p. 6, Lewis 8XYJQFMV p. 86, Peterson UWCY55NG p. 52, Cuthbert BVP63L4A pp. 3 and 5, Haugen I9TIJAC6 p. 11, Ross and Leveritt 3U9Q26V7 p. 17, Marrier XAFUBSPI abstract). Voice labels were checked against `docs/method-baseline.md`.

Counts: 58 claims checked. 36 OK, 20 FIX, 2 REMOVE. 8 of the FIXes block publication.

## 1. Claim table

B = blocking. Section numbers refer to the note.

| # | Claim (note section) | Verdict | Evidence with locator | Exact correction |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | S2 BL1: floor of one heavy lower-body session per game week, early week, load high, sets cut [supported direction; floor] | FIX | Ronnestad 2011 abstract (1/wk kept strength and 40-m sprint, n = 7 per group); Spiering 2021 abstract; but Issurin in-season entry (PDF p. 109, Fig 3.8) prescribes **two** strength key-workouts, and Hoffman 2003 used 2/wk | Add: "Issurin's in-season template uses two strength key-workouts; one is the tested minimum (soccer, n = 7 per group), not the template." Keep the tag. |
| 2 | S2 BL2: one true max-velocity exposure every game week [contested on day count, supported on direction] | FIX (B) | Direction rests on a [contested] entry (residual table), Cuthbert p. 3 which cites Issurin (ref 53) so is not independent, and Saldanha 2026 (uncontrolled, RAST). Against: Ronnestad 2011 held 40-m sprint with 1 lift/wk plus normal soccer and no dedicated max-V work; Ross and Leveritt p. 17 say short-sprint detraining is "less severe than may have been reasonably anticipated" | Retag "[contested; no football data]". Rewrite the position clause as "Inference: prioritize positions that rarely reach top speed in games (no source tests this)." |
| 3 | S2 BL3: heaviest lifting AND practice Tue and Wed; light late [supported for the shape] | FIX (B) | Issurin in-season entry: two strength key-workouts Tue/Wed AM, key practice Thursday PM ("substantial or big" load), only the pre-game session load-restricted (Sunday game). Entry's own Saturday shift: lifts Sun/Mon, key practice Wednesday. Wellman p. 6: Tuesday planned highest practice load (one program). Lewis p. 86: Tue/Wed closest to game demands for linemen | The sources do not agree on where the heaviest practice sits. Move to section 4 as a disagreement. Bottom line: "Heaviest lifting early in the week and the last high-volume practice no later than Wednesday for a Saturday game; volume, not intensity, comes down from Thursday. [Issurin's template (rugby league, Baker 2001) and one D-I program's practice data agree on early-heavy, late-light; they differ on the exact day; descriptive only in college football]" |
| 4 | S2 BL3: at least 48 h between the last heavy or high-volume session and kickoff | FIX (B) | No source prescribes a gap to kickoff. Issurin's 28-30 h is strength key-workout to key practice (entry, PDF p. 109). Verkhoshansky central-peripheral entry: high-CNS work needs "at least 48 hours" recovery if no restorative methods (printed p. 15), which is session spacing. Pritchard 2015 abstract: 2-4 days cessation for peak max strength (strength athletes) | Label "Inference:" and give the chain: "Inference: 48 h is drawn from Verkhoshansky's 48 h recovery after high-CNS work and Pritchard 2015's 2-4 days of cessation before a strength peak; no source tests a gap to kickoff." |
| 5 | S2 BL3 vs S3 and S5: fast force down 72-96 h post-game; heavy work Tue/Wed | FIX (B) | Norris brief p. 2: RFD 0-50 ms down 25.8/17.8/16.9% at 48/72/96 h. Cosio brief p. 8: early hamstring RTD and sprint time still impaired at 72 h. Saturday game puts Tuesday at about 72 h, Wednesday at about 96 h | Add to section 4: "Unresolved: the heavy early-week days fall inside the 72-96 h window in which soccer and AFL data show fast force still depressed. Either the early-week lift is done on incompletely recovered players by design (Issurin's model), or high-velocity work waits until Wednesday. No source tests this in football." Add as a Question for Eric. |
| 6 | S2 BL4: CMJ strategy metrics (mRSI or RSImod, FT:CT), no arm swing, own norm, split by position and starter status; not jump height or ACWR [supported direction; small samples] | FIX | Lewis pp. 96-97 (n = 5), Gathercole p. 7 (n = 8) support. Heishman pp. 6-9: several phase-duration and RFD variables failed reliability (CV > 20%, ICC < 0.70); p. 5: FT:CT less reliable with arm swing; p. 12: study tested reliability, not sensitivity. Norris p. 2: most responsive metric noisiest. Position and starter split rests on Merrigan (off-season) and Aychman (exploratory) | Add: "Strategy metrics are noisier than jump height (Heishman; Norris CV 16.4%), so set thresholds from each player's typical error. Inference: the position and starter split follows from off-season profiles and one exploratory study; no source sets game-week thresholds by group." |
| 7 | S2 BL5: bowl taper about 1-2 weeks, volume cut about 40-60%, intensity kept [supported in other sports; untested in football] | FIX | Bosquet 2007 abstract: 2 wk, 41-60%. Marrier abstract: about 1-2 wk. Haugen p. 11: "2- to 3-week" for strength and power sports. Mujika 2003: 60-90%. Pritchard 2019: about 70% | "about 1 to 3 weeks (Marrier 1-2, Bosquet 2, Haugen 2-3), volume cut about 40-60% (up to 60-90% in Mujika and Padilla), intensity kept." Tag unchanged. |
| 8 | S1: peaking models built on kayakers [supported], one swimmer [untested], throwers [supported] | OK | Realization entry (kayak dosage, PDF p. 124); Popov entry: single swimmer; Bondarchuk entry: sprints, jumps, throws, track and field (PDF p. 175) | Optional: "throwers" to "track and field athletes". |
| 9 | S1 External: Pyne 2009, research concentrated in individual sports and single events, no guide for a team's league season | OK | PubMed 19153861 abstract | none |
| 10 | S1 External: Cuthbert 2024 p. 5, sustaining a peak across a long season unrealistic | OK | BVP63L4A p. 5 (journal p. 184) | none |
| 11 | S1: Afonso, no study tested whether adaptations peaked when predicted (pp. 1, 4) | OK | Afonso brief p. 4 | none |
| 12 | S3: Issurin pre-competitive: cut volume and intense volume, keep frequency, raise max-speed and sport-specific share (PDF p. 105) | OK | Pre-competitive entry, Table 3.5 PDF p. 105 | none |
| 13 | S3: Bondarchuk "somewhat lesser volume to maintain" (PDF p. 175) | OK | Bondarchuk entry | none |
| 14 | S3 External: Mujika and Padilla 2003, keep intensity, volume up to 60-90%, frequency no more than 20% | OK | PubMed 12840640 | none |
| 15 | S3 External: Bosquet 2007, 27 studies, mostly endurance, 2 wk, 41-60%, no intensity or frequency change | FIX | PubMed 17762369 confirms 27 of 182, 2 wk, 41-60%. "Mostly endurance" is not in the abstract | "(abstract; 27 studies; sports not listed in the abstract, mostly endurance per the evidence file)" |
| 16 | S3 External: Pritchard 2019, only the higher-intensity taper improved IMTP and FT:CT | FIX (B) | PubMed 30204523: "No significant changes were found between tapers"; higher-intensity taper gave "small effect-size increases"; 1-week taper, about 70% volume cut | "(abstract; crossover, 11 strength-trained men, 1-week taper, about 70% volume cut): the tapers did not differ significantly; only the higher-intensity taper showed small effect-size gains in IMTP relative peak force and CMJ FT:CT." |
| 17 | S3: Issurin residuals, max strength 30 ± 5 d, speed 5 ± 3 d, no sample reported [contested] (PDF p. 35) | OK | Residual entry, Table 1.6 | none |
| 18 | S3: speed rests on "very delicate and highly precise neuro-muscular interactions" (PDF pp. 35-36) | OK | Residual entry | none |
| 19 | S3: Fleck and Kraemer via Issurin, strength held 14-16 wk then drops [supported], "the only in-season figure in the library" | OK | In-season entry PDF pp. 108-109 | none (the library claim is right; see #45 for the section 6 contradiction) |
| 20 | S3 External: Ronnestad 2011, 1/wk kept strength and 40-m sprint for 12 wk; 1 every 2 wk lost both (n = 7 per group) | OK | PubMed 21873897. Omitted: jump height did not change in either group | Optional add: "jump height did not change in either group", which matters for BL4 (CMJ height missed a strength and sprint loss). |
| 21 | S3 External: Spiering 2021, strength held up to 32 wk on 1 session, 1 set per exercise, if relative load kept; data too thin for athletes | OK | PubMed 33629972 ("at least in younger populations") | none |

Or cut (see cut list). |

It omits that the late mini-block holds the week's heaviest practice (Thursday PM, "substantial or big") | Add "with the week's key practice late (Thursday for a Sunday game)". See #3. |

**Top problems:**
1. **Bottom line 3 misreads Issurin.** In the Issurin library entry (PDF p. 109, Fig 3.8), the two strength sessions fall on Tuesday and Wednesday mornings. The week's heaviest practice is Thursday afternoon, and only the pre-game session is light. The entry's own shift for a Saturday game moves the lifts to Sunday and Monday and the key practice to Wednesday. The note's "heaviest lifting and practice Tuesday and Wednesday" is filed under "sources agree", but Issurin and the college practice data (Wellman p. 6, Lewis p. 86) actually disagree on where the heaviest practice sits. It belongs in "Where they disagree".
2. **The note contradicts itself on post-game recovery.** It cites Norris (fast force still down 16.9% at 96 h) and Cosio (hamstring force and sprint still impaired at 72 h), and says this window transfers to football. After a Saturday game, Tuesday is about 72 h out and Wednesday about 96 h, which is exactly where bottom line 3 puts the heavy work. The note never reconciles this. It needs a stated tension and a question for Eric.
3. **The 48 h gap before kickoff is labelled supported, but no source prescribes it.** Issurin's 28-30 h runs from the last strength session to the key practice. Verkhoshansky's 48 h is spacing between hard sessions. It should be relabelled Inference, with that chain stated.
4. **The note treats a copy of Issurin as independent agreement.** The course's 30/30/5-day numbers are Issurin's own table reproduced in the course slides (week1-lecture p. 66). The same class-1 transcript also says aerobic fitness is gained and lost quickly. So "matches Issurin, conflicts with class-4" is circular, and Question 3 needs rewriting.
5. **Hedges lost or sources misdescribed:**
   - **Pritchard 2019:** the abstract says "no significant changes between tapers", which the note drops.
   - **Saldanha 2026:** the strength that held is hip adductor and abductor strength, and "max velocity" comes from a repeated-sprint test (RAST). Saldanha also does not justify the "one heavy exposure" in the bye-week line.
   - **Peterson p. 52:** it reports differences between position groups, not change within each group from baseline.
   - **Section 6:** it says the only in-season detraining figure is 14-16 weeks, which contradicts the note's own Hoffman 2003 paragraph.
6. **Bottom line 2 (weekly max-velocity exposure) should be tagged contested, not supported, on direction.** Cuthbert's speed point cites Issurin, so it is not independent. Ronnestad kept 40-m sprint speed with one lift a week and no dedicated max-velocity work.

**What checked out:**
- All 12 confidence tags on the book entries match the library.
- Every external number I checked matches its abstract or Zotero page, apart from the hedges above. That covers Ronnestad, Bosquet 2007, Vachon, Spiering, Mujika and Padilla 2003 and 2000, Pritchard 2015, Pyne, Hoffman 2003, Marrier, Wellman, Lewis, Cuthbert, Ross and Leveritt, and Haugen.
- The Explicit and Inferred labels match `method-baseline.md`.

**Not fully confirmed:**
- Aychman's n = 39 appears in the evidence map but not in the library brief.
- Haugen's sentence about sprinters seeing smaller taper gains was only partly re-found on p. 11.

**Missing counter-evidence (11 items listed in the file).** The main ones:
- Bosquet 2013 and Ross and Leveritt: power and short-sprint losses are mild after stopping training.
- Heishman: timing-based CMJ metrics are less reliable, which bottom line 4 needs as a noise caveat.
- Haugen: a 2-3 week taper for strength and power sports, against bottom line 5's 1-2 weeks.
- The bottom line has no aerobic or conditioning line, although Eric's class-4 slide and Mujika and Padilla 2000 both say aerobic fitness is lost fastest.

**Length:** the body is about 2,500 words against a target of about 1,600. The cut list saves about 620 words without losing a claim Eric needs, mostly from sections 3, 5 and 6. Switching the long library links to short aliases would save roughly another rendered page.

I've sent the full review to the agent that launched me. The verdict on the peaking and taper note is **FIX-FIRST**: it isn't ready for Eric yet. The review is in `docs/synthesis/_work/review_peaking_synthesis_opus.md`. That is the only file I created; I didn't edit or commit the note.

I checked 59 claims: 35 are OK, 22 need a fix and 2 should be removed. Nine of the fixes block publication. The main problems:

1. **Bottom line 3 misreads Issurin.** His template puts the heaviest practice late in the week (Thursday for a Sunday game), not on Tuesday and Wednesday. On that point he disagrees with the college practice data (Wellman, Lewis), so it belongs under "where they disagree", not "where the sources agree".
2. **The note contradicts itself on recovery after a game.** It cites evidence that fast force stays down 72 to 96 hours after a match. After a Saturday game, that window covers the Tuesday and Wednesday heavy days it recommends, and the note never reconciles the two.
3. **The "48 hours before kickoff" rule has no source behind it.** It is the writer's own reasoning and needs the "Inference:" label.
4. **Agreement between Eric's course and Issurin is circular.** The course's 30/30/5-day figures are Issurin's own table copied into the slides, so they aren't independent support. Question 3 for Eric needs rewriting to match.
5. **Several sources have lost hedges or are misdescribed.** This applies to Pritchard 2019, Saldanha 2026 and Peterson. The "weekly max-velocity exposure" bottom line should be tagged contested, not supported. One line in section 6 contradicts the note's own Hoffman 2003 paragraph.

All 12 confidence tags on the library book entries match, and every external number I checked matches its abstract or page. Two small things I couldn't fully confirm: Aychman's sample of 39 isn't in the library brief, and I only partly re-found Haugen's sentence about sprinters.

On length, the body is about 2,500 words against a target of about 1,600. The cut list in the review saves about 620 words without losing a claim Eric needs. Switching the long library links to short names would save roughly another page when the note is displayed.
